title: Data Types: Numbers, Text and True/False
oneLiner: Every value in a program has a type that decides how it's stored in bits and what you can do with it, and a fixed-size integer can overflow.
keyTakeaway: A data type tells the computer how to read a pattern of bits: as a whole number, a decimal, a piece of text or true/false. Fixed-size integers such as C#'s 32-bit int have a largest value, and going past it wraps around to a negative number (integer overflow) unless you check. Python's int simply grows. Text is stored as numbers too, one code per character.
explanation:
Memory only holds bits, so the same 32 bits could be a whole number, a decimal number or four letters. A variable is a named place that holds a value, and its data type says how to interpret that value's bits and which operations make sense: you can multiply numbers but not true/false values, and adding two pieces of text joins them. C# makes you (or the compiler) decide each variable's type up front and checks it before the program runs (static typing). Python decides at run time from whatever value the variable currently holds (dynamic typing), so the same name can hold a number now and text later.

The everyday types are: integers (whole numbers, int in both languages), floating-point numbers (decimals such as 3.75, double in C# and float in Python, covered in Floating Point: IEEE-754), booleans (true or false, the result of any comparison such as age >= 18), characters and strings (text, stored as a number per character, covered in Text Encoding), and collections that hold many values (lists and arrays, dictionaries).

Integers are where types bite. A C# int is 32 bits, so it can hold 2^32 different values, split between negatives and positives: -2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647 (Bits, Bytes & Number Bases explains the two's complement trick behind negatives). Add 1 to the largest int and the bits roll over like a car's odometer, giving the most negative int. That's integer overflow, and by default C# does it silently; wrap the code in checked { } and it throws an OverflowException instead. A long is 64 bits and pushes the limit to about 9.2 quintillion. Python's int has no fixed size: it grows to as many bits as the number needs, so it never overflows, at some cost in speed.
